catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-ipolyi:
Arnold Ipolyi, whose family name was originally Stummer, was bishop of Grosswardein, now Nagy-Várad, born at Ipoly-Keszi on 20 October 1823 and dead at Grosswardein on 2 December 1886. At thirteen he joined the students of the Gran archdiocese, studied at Presburg and Tyrnau, and finished at Vienna's Pazmaneum, where he heard theology for four years. He entered Gran seminary in 1844, took minor orders in 1845, and was made priest in 1847.

After tutoring for Baron Mednyánszky, serving as curate at Komorn-Sankt-Peter, preaching at Presburg, and a spell as parish priest of Zohor, he turned increasingly to history and art history. His Hungarian Mythology of 1854, first fruit of that work, treats Hungary's ancient religion. The entry follows a bishop-scholar who gathered a nation's pagan past while serving its parishes and diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-august-roskov:
August Roskovanyi was Bishop of Neutra, a doctor of philosophy and theology born at Szenna in 1807 who died in 1892. He studied with the Piarists at Kis-Szeben, took philosophy at Eger and theology at Pesth, and finished at the Augustineum in Vienna. Ordained in 1831, he rose through the Eger seminary as prefect, vice-rector, and rector. He became a cathedral canon in 1836, then climbed the ladder of sees. He served as auxiliary bishop in 1847, Bishop of Waitzen in 1851, and Bishop of Neutra in 1859.

He was made a Roman count, a prelate, and an assistant at the papal throne, and his charity showed in foundations worth several hundred thousand gulden. As a writer he worked in Latin, producing multi-volume works. They covered the Roman primacy, mixed marriages, marriage law, the church's freedom from civil power, clerical celibacy, and the Immaculate Conception. The entry lists them as his chief scholarly fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-szenti:
Martin Szentivanyi was born at Szentivan on 20 October 1633 and died at Nagy-Szombat on 5 March 1708. He joined the Jesuits in 1653 and taught Scripture five years at Vienna and Nagy-Szombat, mathematics and philosophy nine years, and canon law and theology seven years. He served seven years as chancellor of Nagy-Szombat University.

For nine successive years he governed the Pasmaneum in Vienna and the academy at Nagy-Szombat. His many writings appeared in Hungarian, Latin, German, and Slovak, some translated into French. Chief among them were Curiosiora et selectiora variarum scientiarum miscellanea of 1689, a right method of interpreting Scripture of 1696, a Hungarian chronology summary of 1697, and Doctrinae fidei christianae of 1708. He also wrote against Lutherans in Lutheranicum numquam et nusquam of 1702 and fifty reasons for choosing Roman Catholicism alone among modern faiths, published in 1701.
doe-osti-2587978-optimizing-facility-ope:
Benjamin Ford, Emily Wendel, Timothy Yoder, and V Chandan of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote this final report, PNNL-33364, in January 2025. It closes an Environmental Security Technology Certification Program demonstration, project EW19-5300. The team applied machine learning to the Army Reserve's Enterprise Building Control System, which runs heating, cooling, and ventilation across many reserve facilities.

The idea is to spot waste and faults in building operations from the control system's own data, instead of sending people building to building. A long section covers data quality assessment, the unglamorous work that decides whether the learning can succeed. The team measured how much data each time series was missing, and removed outliers before training, since stray points drag model accuracy down. Performance and cost assessments follow, along with the implementation issues a rollout would face across the Army Reserve estate.
podcast-dannyjones-voHv-6EJkYI:
Engineer Chris Dunn joins Danny Jones to link Tesla tech to the Great Pyramid of Egypt. Dunn has long argued the pyramid was a power plant, not a tomb. His new proof, as the title frames it, ties that plant to Tesla's dream of free power.

Dunn walks through the shafts and rooms he says channeled power from the earth. He draws the line from that plant to Tesla's towers and wireless plans. Jones asks what test could prove the plant once ran. Listeners who love the pyramid power case get its full form here. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
